claims.claim: Ex 12:1–2 makes the month of the Exodus the beginning of months: "This month shall be unto you the beginning of months: it shall be the first month of the year to you." The month is Abib (13:4), i.e. Nisan.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 12:1–2; 13:4, read in full; Josephus Ant. 2.14.6 (Xanthicus = Pharmuthi = Nisan); Philo QE I.1 (the first month reckoned from the vernal equinox).

claims.claim: The lamb is taken on the 10th day of the month and kept until the 14th, when the whole assembly kills it "between the evenings"; it is a male, one year old, without blemish, from the sheep or the goats (12:3–6).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 12:3–6, read in full; K&D (שׂה "a young one, either sheep or goats"; תמים "integer, uninjured, without bodily fault"; one year old, ἐνιαύσιος LXX); BDB pesach H6453 sense 2.

claims.claim: The blood is struck on the two side posts and the upper door post (lintel) of the houses where the lamb is eaten, applied with hyssop; none is to go out of the door of his house until the morning (12:7, 22).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 12:7, 22, read in full; Josephus Ant. 2.14.6 (houses purified with blood using hyssop).

claims.claim: The meal is roast with fire (not sodden with water, not raw), eaten with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, in haste, with loins girded, shoes on feet, staff in hand; nothing is to remain until the morning, and what remains is burnt with fire (12:8–11).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 12:8–11, read in full; Jubilees 49:12–13 (roast on fire, head with inwards and feet, no bone broken).

claims.claim: The name *pesach* is explained in the text by "pass over" (12:13, 23, 27), but the word more likely means "protect" (a "protective offering"), with the Assyrian *pašâḫu* "soothe, placate" as a parallel. The meaning is not settled.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 12:13, 23, 27 (the text's own etymology); Calvin ("a passing-over... of God Himself"); BDB pesach H6453 (from פסח, with reference to Ex 12:13; Assyrian pašâḫu "soothe, placate"); Bible Odyssey ("pesakh more likely means 'protect'"). See §8.1.

claims.claim: The plague is announced as judgement on Egypt's gods as well as its firstborn: "I will pass through the land of Egypt this night, and will smite all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, both man and beast; and against all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgment: I am the LORD" (12:12).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 12:12, read in full; Jubilees 48:5 ("on all their idols the Lord took vengeance and burned them with fire").

claims.claim: The blood is a sign for the houses: "when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and the plague shall not be upon you to destroy you, when I smite the land of Egypt" (12:13).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 12:13, read in full; Jubilees 49:3 (the blood on the lintels as a sign, so the powers "should pass by").

claims.claim: The text distinguishes the LORD from "the destroyer" (הַמַּשְׁחִית, 12:23): the LORD passes through and passes over, and "will not suffer the destroyer to come in unto your houses to smite you." Whether the destroyer is an angel, a personification of the plague, or the LORD's action under another name is not stated.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 12:23, read in full (the distinction is in the text; the identity is not). See §8.2.

claims.claim: The Passover is a memorial ordinance for ever: "this day shall be unto you for a memorial; and ye shall keep it a feast to the LORD throughout your generations; ye shall keep it a feast by an ordinance for ever" (12:14; cf. vv. 17, 24).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 12:14, 17, 24, read in full; Jubilees 49:8 (an eternal ordinance engraved on the heavenly tablets).

claims.claim: Seven days of unleavened bread follow: leaven is put away on the first day; whoever eats leavened bread from the first to the seventh day is cut off from Israel; the first and seventh days are holy convocations, with no work except food preparation (12:15–20).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 12:15–20, read in full; BDB matsah H4682 (the feast of unleavened bread for 7 days after Passover).

claims.claim: Passover and Unleavened Bread are distinct observances in the law: Ex 23:14–15 and 34:18 mention the Feast of Unleavened Bread but not Passover at all; Deut 16 mentions both; Lev 23:5–8 and Num 28:16–25 ordain a Passover offering on the 14th day of the first month, followed by seven days of unleavened bread.
claims.evidence: Bible Odyssey, read in full (the legal sources differ); KJV Ex 23:14–15; 34:18; Lev 23:5–8; Num 28:16–25; Deut 16 (cited from the article's survey).

claims.claim: Moses communicates the ordinance to the elders of Israel (12:21–27) — take a lamb, strike the blood, do not go out till morning, teach the children the meaning — and the people bowed their heads and worshipped, and did as commanded (12:27–28).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 12:21–28, read in full; Calvin (from v. 21 Moses "only relates historically" what was required "on a particular occasion").

claims.claim: The ordinance of the Passover (12:43–49): no stranger eats of it; a bought servant, circumcised, may eat; a sojourner or hired servant may not; it is eaten in one house, none of the flesh carried out, no bone broken (12:46); a stranger who wishes to keep it must circumcise every male; "one law shall be to him that is homeborn, and unto the stranger that sojourneth among you" (12:49).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 12:43–49, read in full; NETS 12:43–49 ("This is the law of the pascha... There shall be one law for the local inhabitant and for the guest").

claims.claim: K&D's reading: the Passover is "the first or foundation law for the congregation of Jehovah", and "the creation of Israel as the people of Jehovah (Isaiah 43:15) commenced with the institution of the Passover" — the festival lays "the foundation for Israel's birth into the new life of grace and fellowship with God".
claims.evidence: K&D on Ex 12:1–2, read in part (verbatim excerpts). A theological reading of the text's placement, not a statement of the text itself; hence Probable, not Established.

claims.claim: Calvin's reading: *pesach* means "a passing-over, not of the people, (as many have falsely thought,) but of God Himself, who passed over the houses of the Israelites without harm, when He slew the first-born in all Egypt" — the passage (*transitus*) of God is equivalent to His leaping over (*transilitio*).
claims.evidence: Calvin, Harmony of the Law, Ex 12:21–28, read in part (verbatim excerpts). Widely held, but an interpretation of the name, not a datum of the text.

claims.claim: In Christian reception the Passover is a sign of spiritual grace analogous to the Lord's Supper: "Christ our passover is sacrificed for us" (1 Cor 5:7); the Passover "was no less than Circumcision a sign of spiritual grace" (Calvin). This is a reception reading, not the Exodus text's own meaning.
claims.evidence: Calvin, Harmony of the Law, Ex 12:1–20, read in part; 1 Cor 5:7 (cited from Calvin's discussion); K&D (the unleavened cakes "symbolical of the new life as cleansed from the leaven of a sinful nature", with 1 Cor 5:7–8).

claims.claim: Jubilees 49 presents the Passover as an eternal ordinance engraved on the heavenly tablets: the lamb is killed on the 14th of the first month before evening and eaten by night on the evening of the 15th (49:1); the blood on the lintels is a sign so that Mastema's powers "should pass by" (49:3); the plague touches no Israelite soul "either of cattle, or man, or dog" (49:4); failure to observe it brings being cut off (49:9).
claims.evidence: Jubilees 49:1–9, read in full (Charles). The claim is about what Jubilees says; its Mastema material is Jubilees' own expansion.

claims.claim: Jubilees 49:16–17 requires the Passover to be eaten only before the sanctuary, by males of 20 years and over — an anachronistic requirement that belongs to Deut 16, not to the Egyptian Passover, and cannot describe the first Passover in Egypt.
claims.evidence: Jubilees 49:16–17, read in full; Deut 16 (the centralised Passover law, cited from the Bible Odyssey survey).

claims.claim: Philo (QE I.1 on Ex 12:2) reads the first month as reckoned from the vernal equinox: the month is "first" and "beginning" by synonymy, first both in order and in power; the Ram is the head of the zodiac, since in it the sun produces the vernal equinox; Nisan is the first month of the vernal/festival calendar and the seventh of the autumnal/civil calendar.
claims.evidence: Philo, Questions and Answers on Exodus I.1, read directly (Marcus, Loeb Suppl. II, 1953, via archive.org).

claims.claim: Philo (QE I.2 on Ex 12:3, 6) poses the question why Moses commands the lamb to be kept from the 10th day of the first month until the 14th, when it is sacrificed.
claims.evidence: Philo, QE I.2, read directly (opening of the section; the answer continues beyond the portion read).

claims.claim: At midnight the LORD smote all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh that sat on his throne to the firstborn of the captive in the dungeon and all the firstborn of cattle; "there was a great cry in Egypt; for there was not a house where there was not one dead" (12:29–30).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 12:29–30, read in full; Jubilees 49:2 (Mastema's powers let loose to slay the firstborn).

claims.claim: Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron by night and said, "Rise up, and get you forth from among my people, both ye and the children of Israel; and go, serve the LORD, as ye have said... and bless me also" (12:31–32).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 12:31–32, read in full; Josephus Ant. 2.14.6 (the Egyptians near the palace persuaded Pharaoh).

claims.claim: The Egyptians urged the people to depart in haste, "for they said, We be all dead men" (12:33); the people took their dough before it was leavened, their kneadingtroughs bound up in their clothes (12:34), and baked unleavened cakes, "for it was not leavened; because they were thrust out of Egypt, and could not tarry" (12:39).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 12:33–34, 39, read in full; NETS 12:39 ("For the Egyptians had thrown them out, and they were unable to remain").

claims.claim: The "spoiling of the Egyptians" (12:35–36) — silver jewels, gold jewels, raiment — was a giving, not a loan: the Egyptians gave willingly because "the LORD gave the people favour in the sight of the Egyptians". Josephus (with Whiston's note) reads the goods as gifts/spoils, not loans, citing Gen 15:14, Ex 3:22, 11:2, Ps 105:37.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 12:35–36 ("the LORD gave the people favour"); Josephus Ant. 2.14.6 with Whiston's note, read in full. Probable because the Hebrew נתן/שאל allows the "borrow" rendering the KJV's neighbours use; the gift reading is the better one, not a certainty.

claims.claim: The departure is from Rameses to Succoth, "about six hundred thousand on foot that were men, beside children" (12:37). The figure is the text's own; a total population of about 2 million (adding wives and children) is an inference from it, not the text's number.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 12:37, read in full; K&D (600,000 men on foot implies about 2 million souls); Josephus Ant. 2.15.2 ("600,000 men of war age").

claims.claim: "A mixed multitude went up also with them; and flocks, and herds, even very much cattle" (12:38). The multitude's composition is not specified.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 12:38, read in full.

claims.claim: The 430 years (12:40) differ between the textual traditions: MT, "the sojourning of the children of Israel, who dwelt in Egypt, was four hundred and thirty years"; LXX (NETS), "during which they dwelt in the land, Egypt, and in the land of Chanaan was four hundred and thirty years" — the LXX adds "and in the land of Chanaan".
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 12:40, read in full; NETS Ex 12:40, read directly ("land of Chanaan was four hundred and thirty").

claims.claim: The 430 years are read in two ways: 430 years in Egypt alone (MT), or 430 years from Abraham's entry into Canaan to the Exodus, with 215 years in Egypt (LXX; Josephus Ant. 2.15.2: "430 years after Abraham came into Canaan, 215 years after Jacob entered Egypt"). The two readings are not reconciled in this dossier.
claims.evidence: Josephus Ant. 2.15.2, read in full; NETS Ex 12:40, read directly; KJV Ex 12:40. See §7.2.

claims.claim: Ex 12:42 — "a night to be much observed unto the LORD" (KJV) — is better rendered "a preservation-night of the Lord": the hapax legomenon שִׁמֻּרִים means "preservation" (from שָׁמַר, to keep, to preserve), not "celebration". NETS renders "vigil".
claims.evidence: K&D on Ex 12:42, read in part (verbatim excerpt: the apax legomenon "does not mean 'celebration'... but 'preservation'"); NETS Ex 12:42 ("It is a vigil for the Lord"), read directly. Probable because the lexical argument is strong but the KJV's rendering has long standing.

claims.claim: The departure took place on the 15th day of the first month: Josephus dates the leaving of Egypt to "the month Xanthicus, on the fifteenth day" (Ant. 2.15.1), and Num 33:3 states the departure from Rameses was "on the fifteenth day of the first month". Exodus 12 itself does not state the 15th explicitly.
claims.evidence: Josephus Ant. 2.15.1, read in full; Num 33:3 (cited as a connection, §11). Probable because the date is established by the neighbouring texts, not by Ex 12 itself.

claims.claim: Josephus gives the leaders' ages at the Exodus: Moses 80, Aaron 83 (Ant. 2.15.2). The figures agree with Ex 7:7 (Moses 80, Aaron 83 when they spoke to Pharaoh).
claims.evidence: Josephus Ant. 2.15.2, read in full; Ex 7:7 (cited as a cross-check). The claim is about what Josephus (and Ex 7:7) state.

claims.claim: Jubilees 48:14 gives its own figures for the sea's destruction: 1,000,000 Egyptians destroyed, plus 1,000 strong men for one suckling cast into the river. These are Jubilees' expansions, not the Exodus text's figures.
claims.evidence: Jubilees 48:14, read in full (Charles). The claim is about what Jubilees says.

claims.claim: "Sanctify unto me all the firstborn, whatsoever openeth the womb among the children of Israel, both of man and of beast: it is mine" (13:2). The firstborn belong to the LORD.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 13:2, read in full; BDB bekhor H1060 (כָּל־בְּכוֹר, Ex 13:2, 13, 15).

claims.claim: The firstborn consecration is explained by the tenth plague: "the LORD slew all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, both the firstborn of man, and the firstborn of beast: therefore I sacrifice to the LORD all that openeth the matrix, being males; but all the firstborn of my children I redeem" (13:15).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 13:15, read in full.

claims.claim: The redemption law (13:11–16): every firstling of an ass is redeemed with a lamb, and if not redeemed its neck is broken; every firstborn son is redeemed; when the son asks "What is this?", the answer is "By strength of hand the LORD brought us out from Egypt, from the house of bondage" (13:14).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 13:11–16, read in full; NETS 13:12–13 ("Everything opening the womb of a donkey you will exchange for a sheep").

claims.claim: The sign "upon thine hand" and "for a memorial between thine eyes" (13:9, 16) is the origin of the later Jewish practice of tefillin (phylacteries). The connection is reception: Exodus commands a sign and a memorial, not a physical object.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 13:9, 16, read in full (the sign language); the tefillin identification is the later tradition's reading, noted here as reception.

claims.claim: The departure is in the month Abib (13:4): "This day came ye out in the month Abib." Abib is the spring month, Nisan, the first month of the festival calendar.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 13:4, read in full; Philo QE I.1 (Nisan, the first month of the vernal calendar); Bible Odyssey (Nisan = Abib, Ex 13:4; 23:15; 34:18; Deut 16:1).

claims.claim: God led them NOT by the way of the land of the Philistines, "although that was near; for God said, Lest peradventure the people repent when they see war, and they return to Egypt" (13:17). Philo adds a second reason: also to test them (Vita Mosis I.164).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 13:17, read in full; Philo, Vita Mosis I.164, read in full (fear of war and return; "also to test them").

claims.claim: The route taken is the roundabout way: "God led the people about, through the way of the wilderness of the Red Sea" (13:18); NETS, "God led the people a roundabout way towards the wilderness, towards the Red Sea".
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 13:18, read in full; NETS Ex 13:18 ("towards the Red Sea"), read directly.

claims.claim: Joseph's bones are carried out of Egypt (13:19), fulfilling the oath of Gen 50:25: "God will surely visit you; and ye shall carry up my bones away hence with you."
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 13:19, read in full; Gen 50:25 (the oath, cited as a connection, §11).

claims.claim: The itinerary names Succoth and Etham — "they took their journey from Succoth, and encamped in Etham, in the edge of the wilderness" (13:20) — but neither place is identified with confidence.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 13:20, read in full (the names are stated); no identification was verified in this session. See §7.3.

claims.claim: The pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night goes before the people "to give them light; to go by day and night", and "he took not away the pillar of the cloud by day, nor the pillar of fire by night, from before the people" (13:21–22).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 13:21–22, read in full; Philo, Vita Mosis I.166 (the pillar as "one of the ministers of the mighty King, an unseen messenger").

claims.claim: Josephus adds two details to the departure: the route was chosen also to bring the people to Sinai, and the unleavened loaves lasted 30 days (Ant. 2.15.1); the feast of unleavened bread is kept for 8 days in his account.
claims.evidence: Josephus Ant. 2.15.1, read in full. The claim is about what Josephus says.

claims.claim: NETS Ex 13:18 renders the Israelites' going up as "in the fifth generation" — the LXX's reading of Hebrew חֲמֻשִׁים *hamushim* ("armed, harnessed", KJV "harnessed") as "fifth". The MT's "armed" is the better reading; the LXX's is a witness to Alexandrian understanding.
claims.evidence: NETS Ex 13:18 ("in the fifth generation"), read directly; KJV Ex 13:18 ("harnessed"). See §3.2.

claims.claim: The encampment is specified with three names: "before Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, over against Baal-zephon: before it shall ye encamp by the sea" (14:2). NETS renders Pi-hahiroth as "the village" and the names as Magdolos and Beelsepphon.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 14:2, read in full; NETS Ex 14:2 ("opposite the village between Magdolos and between the sea, opposite Beelsepphon"), read directly.

claims.claim: The locations Pi-hahiroth, Migdol and Baal-zephon are not identified with confidence. JFB proposes Pi-hahiroth as Bedea ("the mouth of the defile"); Clarke proposes "the mouth, strait, or bay of Chiroth" (Shaw's valley from Etham to the Red Sea). Both are 19th-century proposals, not established identifications.
claims.evidence: JFB on Ex 14:2, read via BibleHub excerpts; Clarke on Ex 14:2, read via BibleHub excerpts; JFB: "The locality of this famous passage has not yet been, and probably never will be, satisfactorily fixed." See §7.3.

claims.claim: God's stated purpose in the turn south is that Pharaoh will think Israel "entangled in the land" and the wilderness has shut them in (14:3), "and I will be honoured upon Pharaoh, and upon all his host; that the Egyptians may know that I am the LORD" (14:4; cf. vv. 17–18).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 14:3–4, 17–18, read in full; JFB (the object was "to entice Pharaoh to pursue").

claims.claim: Pharaoh's pursuit force is 600 chosen chariots, all the chariots of Egypt, horsemen and army (14:7, 9). Josephus inflates it to 600 chariots, 50,000 horsemen and 200,000 footmen (Ant. 2.15.3); Philo gives cavalry, darters, slingers, archers and 600 scythe-bearing chariots (Vita Mosis I.168). The text's figure is the 600 chosen chariots.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 14:7, 9, read in full; Josephus Ant. 2.15.3, read in full; Philo, Vita Mosis I.168, read in full. The claim distinguishes the text's figure from the retellings'.

claims.claim: The people's complaint (14:11–12): "Because there were no graves in Egypt, hast thou taken us away to die in the wilderness? wherefore hast thou dealt thus with us, to carry us forth out of Egypt?... it had been better for us to serve the Egyptians, than that we should die in the wilderness." Philo paraphrases the complaint (Vita Mosis I.171).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 14:11–12, read in full; Philo, Vita Mosis I.171, read in full.

claims.claim: Moses' reply (14:13–14): "Fear ye not, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD, which he will shew to you to day: for the Egyptians whom ye have seen to day, ye shall see them again no more for ever. The LORD shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace."
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 14:13–14, read in full; NETS 14:13–14 ("Take courage! Stand, and see the deliverance from God... you shall not ever again see them time without end").

claims.claim: The command to advance and to divide the sea: "speak unto the children of Israel, that they go forward" (14:15); "lift thou up thy rod, and stretch out thine hand over the sea, and divide it: and the children of Israel shall go on dry ground through the midst of the sea" (14:16).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 14:15–16, read in full; NETS 14:16 ("raise your rod, and stretch out your hand over the sea, and break it apart").

claims.claim: The angel of God and the pillar move from before the camp to behind it (14:19–20); there is darkness and cloud to the Egyptians and light to Israel, "so that the one came not near the other all the night". JFB identifies the angel of God with the pillar of cloud (Ex 13:21).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 14:19–20, read in full (the movement is stated); JFB on Ex 14:19 ("the angel of God — that is, the pillar of cloud"), read via BibleHub excerpts. Probable because the identification is JFB's, not the text's.

claims.claim: The wind is the stated means, and the traditions disagree on its direction: MT/KJV, "the LORD caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all that night" (14:21); LXX/NETS, "the Lord drew off the sea by a strong south wind during the whole night". The wind is named three times as the means (14:21; 15:8, 10).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 14:21, read in full; NETS Ex 14:21 ("strong south wind"), read directly; KJV Ex 15:8, 10 (the wind in the Song). See §3.2.

claims.claim: The crossing: "the children of Israel went into the midst of the sea upon the dry ground: and the waters were a wall unto them on their right hand, and on their left" (14:22; repeated v. 29).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 14:22, 29, read in full; NETS 14:22 ("the water became a wall for them on the right and a wall on the left").

claims.claim: In the morning watch the LORD "looked unto the host of the Egyptians through the pillar of fire and of the cloud, and troubled the host of the Egyptians, and took off their chariot wheels, that they drave them heavily" (14:24–25); the Egyptians say, "Let us flee from the face of Israel; for the LORD fighteth for them against the Egyptians."
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 14:24–25, read in full; NETS 14:24–25 ("he threw the camp of the Egyptians into disarray... he bound together the axles of their chariots").

claims.claim: The waters return and cover "the chariots, and the horsemen, and all the host of Pharaoh that came into the sea after them; there remained not so much as one of them" (14:28).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 14:28, read in full; NETS 14:28 ("Not even one of them remained!"); Josephus Ant. 2.16.3 ("not one man left to be a messenger").

claims.claim: "Thus the LORD saved Israel that day out of the hand of the Egyptians; and Israel saw the Egyptians dead upon the sea shore" (14:30); "the people feared the LORD, and believed the LORD, and his servant Moses" (14:31).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 14:30–31, read in full; NETS 14:30–31 ("Israel saw the Egyptians dead along the shore of the sea... the people feared the Lord and trusted God and Moyses, his attendant").

claims.claim: The crossing's location is debated (R2): the main proposals are the Gulf of Suez (Overstreet; JFB's Mount Attakah / mouth of Wady Tawarik), Lake Ballah (Hoffmeier, with Bietak), Lake Timsah or the northern Bitter Lakes, the southern Bitter Lakes, Lake Menzaleh, and Lake Sirbonis (Brugsch). No proposal is established.
claims.evidence: Overstreet, TMSJ 14/1 (2003), read in full: "Proposed sites for the crossing include: Lake Sirbonis, Lake Menzaleh, Lake Ballah, Lake Timsah or the northern Bitter Lakes, or the southern Bitter Lakes." Overstreet's own position is the Gulf of Suez. JFB on Ex 14, read in full (Mount Attakah / mouth of Wady Tawarik; "The locality of this famous passage has not yet been, and probably never will be, satisfactorily fixed"). Hoffmeier, "Out of Egypt" (2012), read in full: the el-Ballah lakes are "the most viable candidate for Yam Suf" (Bietak's p3-tjufy). See §7.3.

claims.claim: *Yam-suph* is literally "sea of reeds" (*suph* = reeds/rushes; cf. Ex 2:3, Isa 19:6); the LXX renders it "Red Sea" (*erythra thalassa*), and the Vulgate and KJV follow the versions. No convincing explanation of why the LXX chose "red" is established.
claims.evidence: BDB suph H5488, read directly ("sea of rushes or reeds... which Greek included in wider name θάλασσα Ἐρυθρά, Red Sea"); BDB yam H3220 §2, read directly; NETS Ex 13:18 ("towards the Red Sea"), read directly.

claims.claim: *Yam-suph* covers wider geography than one body of water: 1 Kgs 9:26 places Ezion-geber beside *yam-suph* near Elath (Gulf of Aqaba), and BDB counts the "Red Sea" as named or referred to approximately 66 times in the Hebrew Bible.
claims.evidence: BDB yam H3220 §2, read directly ("'Red Sea' named or referred to approximately 66 t.; יַם־סוּף clearly of [the] Elanitic Gulf, 1 Kings 9:26"); KJV 1 Kgs 9:26.

claims.claim: The Song (15:1–18) is the first great song in the Bible: "Then sang Moses and the children of Israel this song unto the LORD" (15:1), sung after the crossing as the response to the deliverance of Ex 14.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 15:1, read in full; Ex 14:30–31 (the deliverance it answers).

claims.claim: The Song's opening theology: "The LORD is a man of war: the LORD is his name" (15:3); "Who is like unto thee, O LORD, among the gods? who is like thee, glorious in holiness, fearful in praises, doing wonders?" (15:11) — answering Ex 12:12's judgement "against all the gods of Egypt".
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 15:3, 11, read in full; KJV Ex 12:12 (the judgement the Song answers).

claims.claim: The Song looks forward to the sanctuary: "Thou shalt bring them in, and plant them in the mountain of thine inheritance, in the place, O LORD, which thou hast made for thee to dwell in, in the Sanctuary, O Lord, which thy hands have established. The LORD shall reign for ever and ever" (15:17–18).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 15:17–18, read in full.

claims.claim: The Song is widely regarded as among the oldest poems in the Hebrew Bible: Cross & Freedman ("The Song of Miriam", JNES 14, 1955; *Canaanite Myth and Hebrew Epic*, 1973) treated it as an early, pre-monarchic poem, and Russell (2007) concludes a 12th-century BCE date. The date is contested — Brenner (BZAW 195, 1991) argues for a post-exilic date — so the early date is not established.
claims.evidence: JFB on Ex 15, read in full ("This song is, by some hundred years, the oldest poem in the world"); K&D on Ex 15, read in full (the song's authenticity and Mosaic authorship "placed beyond all doubt by both the contents and the form"); Noegel (2023), read in full: the poem's date "continues to resist scholarly consensus," with Cross, Freedman and Russell representative of the truly-archaic position (Russell concluding a 12th-century BCE date) and Brenner (1991) representative of the post-exilic position. See §8.4.

claims.claim: The Song's language is considerably older than the surrounding prose narrative: archaic orthography and verbal forms (e.g. *ga'oh ga'ah*, v. 1) and a terse parallelistic structure. Scholars agree the poet loaded the poem with archaic poetic features, though whether they are truly archaic or an archaizing style is disputed.
claims.evidence: K&D on Ex 15, read in full (זמרת "an old poetic form"; the song composed at the time); JFB on Ex 15, read in full (the oldest poem in the world); Noegel (2023), read in full ("all generally agree that the structure is sophisticated and that the poet has loaded the poem with archaic poetic features, whether truly archaic or not"; the poet's use of "'poetic' or 'archaic' 3 m.pl. forms"). Probable because the archaic-vs-archaizing question is unresolved.

claims.claim: The Song is preserved with remarkable uniformity across the Masoretic Text, the Samaritan Pentateuch, and Dead Sea Scroll fragments (4QExod-Levf, 4QpaleoExod-m); the consonantal text shows virtually no significant divergence.
claims.evidence: Second-hand (BibleHub Q&A on Ex 15:1). The DSS fragments were not read directly in this session; the registry's DJD XII entry is not-independently-verified and its recorded scope is 4QGen-b only. Probable because second-hand.

claims.claim: Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a timbrel in her hand, and all the women went out after her with timbrels and dances (15:20); she answered them, "Sing ye to the LORD, for he hath triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider hath he thrown into the sea" (15:21) — repeating 15:1 almost verbatim.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 15:20–21, read in full; NETS 15:20–21 ("Mariam, the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took the tambourine... And Mariam took their lead").

claims.claim: Miriam's song (v. 21) is often called the "Song of Miriam", and its relationship to vv. 1–18 is debated: an independent refrain that the longer song develops, or a summary of the longer song. Cross & Freedman favour the former on an early dating; a late dating makes the latter more feasible.
claims.evidence: The Next Step Bible Study notes ("The exact relationship of the 'Song of Miriam' (v. 21) to the full Song has been a much-debated question"); Noegel (2023), read in full, records Cross & Freedman among those who see the poem as truly archaic, which favours the independent-refrain reading on an early dating, while a late dating makes the summary reading more feasible.

claims.claim: Josephus reports that Moses composed the song "in hexameter verse" and that the Hebrews sang hymns all night (Ant. 2.16.4). The hexameter claim is Josephus' own description, not a modern metrical judgement.
claims.evidence: Josephus Ant. 2.16.4, read in full. The claim is about what Josephus reports.

claims.claim: Philo gives two choruses — men led by Moses, women led by Miriam (Vita Mosis I.180) — and a mechanism for the crossing: a violent south wind, the sea's ebb and flow, Moses smiting the sea with his staff, the parts raised like a wall, a dry road, and a strong north wind bringing the tide back to overwhelm the Egyptians, so that "not even a torchbearer" survived (I.176–179). Philo's south wind agrees with the LXX against the MT's east wind.
claims.evidence: Philo, Vita Mosis I.176–180, read in full. The claim is about what Philo says.

claims.claim: R1, the early date: c. 1446 BCE — 1 Kgs 6:1 (480 years before Solomon's temple, fourth year c. 966 BCE); Amenhotep II as the pharaoh of the Exodus in this model; Jericho City IV c. 1400 (Wood) cited in support.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining Library, "Exodus" (overview article), read in full: the early view dates the exodus to 1446 BC from 1 Kgs 6:1 (480 years before Solomon's fourth year, c. 966 BC), with Thutmose III as the pharaoh of the oppression and Amenhotep II as the pharaoh of the exodus; "The older dating of the fall of Jericho to about 1400 BC" is cited in support. The 480 years may be schematic; no Egyptian record confirms the date.

claims.claim: R1, the late date: c. 1260 BCE — Ramesses II (1279–1213); Pithom and Raamses (Ex 1:11); the 480 years as schematic (12 generations × 40); on the late view the exodus took place about 1270–1260 BCE.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining Library, "Exodus" (overview article), read in full: "Other scholars place the exodus in the 13th century BC, during the long reign of Ramesses II (c. 1279–1213 BC). They begin from the store city of Rameses (Exod 1:11)." On this view "the 480 years of 1 Kgs 6:1 is understood as twelve generations of forty years, a schematic total," and "the exodus took place about 1270–1260 BC." The Merneptah Stele (c. 1208 BC) bounds it (clm-pa-073).

claims.claim: The Merneptah Stele (c. 1208 BCE, Year 5) is the earliest reference to Israel outside the Bible and sets a terminus ante quem: a people called Israel existed in Canaan by c. 1208 BCE, so the Exodus — if it happened — happened before then, allowing for the wilderness period. Both date models must satisfy this.
claims.evidence: Merneptah Stele, verified via the Biblical Archaeology article, read in full (line 27; the people determinative; Petrie 1896; Spiegelberg; JE 31408); Breasted (1906) and ANET 376–378 consulted second-hand for the print history. See §6.1.

claims.claim: The stele cannot confirm the Exodus itself: it records no mass departure, plagues, or drowning — only a claimed victory over a people called Israel in Canaan. Claims that it confirms the Exodus go further than its one line can carry.
claims.evidence: Merneptah Stele line 27, verified via the Biblical Archaeology article, read in full (the inscription's subject is the Libyan victory and the Canaan list).

claims.claim: The 600,000 men (12:37) are stated in the text; whether the figure is literal, schematic, or a later inflation is debated in modern scholarship, and no alternative figure is established. The ~2 million total is an inference from the text's figure, not the text's number.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 12:37, read in full (the figure is stated); K&D (about 2 million souls, as an inference); the modern debate as summarised in §7.4.

claims.claim: The Exodus is the foundational deliverance of Israel: the Passover, the firstborn consecration and the Song are all made perpetual memorials (12:14; 13:3, 9), and the event is cited as the paradigm of salvation throughout the Old Testament and the New Testament (1 Cor 5:7; John 19:36; Heb 11:28–29).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 12:14; 13:3, 9, read in full; the NT citations as surveyed in §8.6 (1 Cor 5:7; John 19:36; Heb 11:28–29).

claims.claim: Jubilees 48 makes Mastema the hidden agent of the Exodus story: Mastema sought to slay Moses on the way (48:2–3, cf. Ex 4:24); Mastema helped the Egyptian sorcerers, who could work evils but not remedies (48:9–10); Mastema urged the pursuit (48:12); Mastema was bound from the 14th to the 18th and loosed on the 19th (48:15–16). This is Jubilees' expansion, not Exodus.
claims.evidence: Jubilees 48:2–3, 9–12, 15–16, read in full (Charles). The claim is about what Jubilees says.

claims.claim: Augustine (City of God XVI.43) counts 144 years from Joseph's death to the Exodus; lists the ten plagues; places the law's giving on the fiftieth day after the Passover lamb, "which is so completely a type of Christ"; reads pascha as "transit" in Hebrew; and notes that Moses did not lead the people into the land — Joshua (Jesus) did.
claims.evidence: Augustine, City of God XVI.43, read in full (Dods, NPNF 1/2, via CCEL). The 144 years are Augustine's computation; the typology is his reading.

connections.note: The first month of 12:2 is named Abib in 13:4; the calendar established at the Passover is the calendar of the departure.
The 14th day of the first month, "between the evenings", is re-ordained as the Passover's date in the festival calendar.
Unleavened bread as "the bread of affliction... for thou camest forth out of the land of Egypt in haste".
"Against all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgment" (12:12) is answered by "Who is like unto thee, O LORD, among the gods?" (15:11).
The blood as a sign (v. 13) and the LORD passing over the door (v. 23) — the same night, the same sign, the same promise.
"A memorial" (12:14) and "Remember this day, in which ye came out from Egypt" (13:3) — the memorial language that structures both chapters.
The Passover kept at Gilgal on the 14th day, the first Passover in the land — the ordinance of Ex 12 fulfilled on entry.
The psalms' retelling of the firstborn's smiting ("smote all the firstborn in Egypt, the chief of their strength") — Ps 78:51.
The psalms' retelling of the firstborn's smiting ("smote all the firstborn in Egypt, the chief of their strength") — Ps 105:36.
The psalms' retelling of the firstborn's smiting ("smote all the firstborn in Egypt, the chief of their strength") — Ps 136:10.
Pharaoh's release ("Rise up, and get you forth") and his reversal ("What is this we have done, that we have let Israel go?") — the pursuit's occasion.
The departure from Rameses on the 15th day of the first month; the itinerary's first station.
Paul's chronology: the law came 430 years after the promise to Abraham — the LXX's scope (Egypt and Canaan), not the MT's.
"Neither shall ye break a bone thereof" fulfilled at the crucifixion: "A bone of him shall not be broken."
The second Passover (Num 9) repeats the rule: "they shall leave none of it unto the morning, nor break any bone of it."
"All the firstborn are mine" (Num 3:13) — the Levites taken in place of the firstborn (Num 3:12, 41, 45).
The sign on the hand and the memorial/frontlets between the eyes — the same language in the Shema's command.
The road not taken (the way of the Philistines) and the turn south (Pi-hahiroth) — the route's two decisions.
Joseph's bones, carried from Egypt, are buried at Shechem — the oath of Gen 50:25 fulfilled.
The pillar of cloud and fire that leads in Ex 13 fills the tabernacle in Ex 40 and leads the wilderness journey.
"Stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD" (14:13) answered by the Song: "I will sing unto the LORD... he is become my salvation" (15:1–2).
The wind in prose ("a strong east wind", 14:21) and in poetry ("with the blast of thy nostrils the waters were gathered together", 15:8).
Dry ground in prose ("the waters were a wall unto them", 14:22) and in poetry ("the children of Israel went on dry land in the midst of the sea", 15:19).
"The waters covered their enemies: there was not one of them left" — the psalm's exact echo of "there remained not so much as one of them".
"The people feared the LORD, and believed" (14:31) — "By faith they passed through the Red sea as by dry land" (Heb 11:29).
The Song of Moses becomes the song of the redeemed: "the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb".
"Who is like unto thee... among the gods?" (15:11) — "Who among the sons of the mighty can be likened unto the LORD?" (Ps 89:6).
"The mountain of thine inheritance... the Sanctuary" (15:17) — "the mountain which his right hand hath purchased" (Ps 78:54).
"The mountain of thine inheritance... the Sanctuary" (15:17) — "let them make me a sanctuary" (Ex 25:8).
"It is the sacrifice of the LORD's passover" (12:27) — "Christ our passover is sacrificed for us" (1 Cor 5:7).
The mixed multitude (12:38) reappears as "the mixt multitude that was among them" whose lusting begins the wilderness complaints (Num 11:4).
The complaint pattern: "were it not better for us to serve the Egyptians?" (14:12) becomes "were it not better for us to return into Egypt?" (Num 14:3–4).
Miriam's timbrels and dances (15:20) — the women's victory dance repeated when Jephthah's daughter comes out "with timbrels and with dances" (Judg 11:34).

date.note: The date of the Exodus is debated (early vs. late); pending research question R1. Chronology is narrative only.
